title: The third incomplete escalation
scenario: Illustrative. Priya, one of your strongest agents on customer empathy, has sent engineering three escalations this month that were missing device logs. Engineering bounced each one back, adding a day to resolution. The engineering manager has messaged you: 'Can you sort out your team's escalation quality?' Priya is also handling the largest share of your hardest accounts.

choices.label: Talk to Priya privately today, show her the three cases, and agree a fix
costs: Treats it as a person problem before checking the process
Priya may feel singled out if others make the same miss
choices.likelyOutcome: Priya's next escalations improve; if the cause was the process, the same gap appears with someone else in a few weeks.

choices.label: Pull the last 30 escalations from the whole team and check how many miss logs
gains: Tests whether it's a person or a system issue
Gives you a baseline to show engineering
costs: Takes an hour or two you may not have
Engineering waits longer for a visible response
choices.likelyOutcome: You learn whether the template, tooling or training is the real gap — often it's a mix.

choices.label: Add a mandatory 'logs attached' field to the escalation form
gains: Prevents the specific failure for everyone
costs: Checkbox may be ticked without logs actually attached
Doesn't address why logs were missed
choices.likelyOutcome: Compliance rises; quality improves only if someone samples whether the logs are the right ones.

choices.label: Reply to the engineering manager first, then decide
gains: Buys time to look at evidence
costs: Can read as deflection if not followed by action
choices.likelyOutcome: Tension drops; outcome depends on what you do next.

relevantConcepts.name: Skill, will or system?
relevantConcepts.explanation: Repeated mistakes usually come from missing skill, low motivation, or a process that makes the mistake easy. The fix differs for each.

relevantConcepts.name: Fix the process before blaming the person
relevantConcepts.explanation: If several capable people could make the same miss, the process is part of the cause.

relevantConcepts.name: Escalation quality
relevantConcepts.explanation: A good escalation lets engineering act within minutes: reproduction steps, logs, impact, and what has been tried.

debrief: There's no single right move. Strong managers often combine B and A: check whether it's a pattern, then coach with specific cases — and tell the engineering manager what they're doing in the meantime (D). Option C helps only if the form change is paired with sampling.
reflectionQuestion: When you see a repeated mistake, what is your default first assumption — person or process?

title: Your portfolio is down 18%
scenario: Illustrative, educational only. You invest monthly in a diversified equity index fund for a goal about twelve years away. After a broad market fall, your statement shows the investment is 18% below its recent peak. Colleagues are discussing moving to fixed deposits 'until things settle'. Nothing about your goal or income has changed.

choices.label: Pause the monthly investment until the market recovers
costs: You stop buying when prices are lower
Requires a second decision about when to restart, which is hard to time
choices.likelyOutcome: Many people restart only after prices have already risen.

choices.label: Sell and move to fixed deposits
costs: May leave the long-term goal underfunded after inflation
choices.likelyOutcome: Emotionally calmer, but the plan changes because of discomfort rather than new information.

choices.label: Continue as planned and check whether your allocation still matches your plan
gains: Rebalancing is a rule, not a prediction
choices.likelyOutcome: The decision is consistent with the plan; outcome still depends on markets, which nobody can predict.

choices.label: Reassess whether your risk capacity has changed (job, goal date, emergency fund)
gains: Separates facts about you from feelings about prices
May reveal a real reason to adjust
costs: Can become a rationalisation for selling
choices.likelyOutcome: If capacity hasn't changed, you return to C with more confidence; if it has, a measured change is reasonable.

relevantConcepts.name: Loss aversion
relevantConcepts.explanation: Falls hurt more than equal gains please, which pushes towards selling.

relevantConcepts.name: Risk tolerance vs risk capacity
relevantConcepts.explanation: Feeling unable to bear risk is different from being financially unable to.

relevantConcepts.name: Anchoring on a price
relevantConcepts.explanation: The 'recent peak' is a reference point, not a fact about future value.

debrief: This is not financial advice. The useful distinction is between changes in your situation (capacity, goal date, cash needs) and changes in how the number feels. D followed by C is the most evidence-led path for many long-horizon investors; B or A can be reasonable if your capacity genuinely changed.
reflectionQuestion: What did you decide your sell conditions were before this fall — and did you write them down?

title: Let the AI agent issue refunds?
scenario: Illustrative. Your team piloted an AI agent that drafts responses to billing tickets. Most drafts were accepted unchanged during the pilot, and handle time fell. Leadership asks whether the agent can now issue small refunds directly, without human approval, to cut response times further.

choices.label: Allow it for refunds under a low threshold, with daily sampling
choices.likelyOutcome: Works if the cases are well-understood and someone owns the sample review.

choices.label: Keep human approval on all refunds
choices.likelyOutcome: Safe on paper; real safety depends on whether approvers read the evidence.

choices.label: Run it in shadow mode first: the agent decides, a human still acts, and you compare
choices.likelyOutcome: You get real data on where it disagrees with humans — usually the edge cases.

choices.label: Decline: refunds stay manual indefinitely
choices.likelyOutcome: Risk is avoided, but the question returns with less of your input.

relevantConcepts.name: Human-in-the-loop placement
relevantConcepts.explanation: Put review where actions are irreversible or costly, and show reviewers the evidence.

relevantConcepts.name: One-way vs two-way doors
relevantConcepts.explanation: Refunds are partly reversible; promises to customers often aren't.

relevantConcepts.name: Automation bias
relevantConcepts.explanation: People tend to over-trust automated outputs, especially when tired or rushed.

debrief: C then A is a common, evidence-building path. B feels safe but can create rubber-stamping. D is defensible for high-value or regulated cases. The key question isn't 'AI or not' but 'what is the cost of an error and how quickly would we notice?'
reflectionQuestion: What evidence would you need to see before giving any system — human or AI — more autonomy?

title: SLA is green, customers are unhappy
scenario: Illustrative. Your first-response SLA has been above target for two months. Customer satisfaction on the same queue has dropped. Your team leads say they're doing exactly what was asked. Your director wants a plan by Friday.

choices.label: Add a resolution-time target alongside first response
gains: Measures what customers feel more directly
costs: A new target can be gamed too (e.g. premature closures)
choices.likelyOutcome: Some improvement; watch reopen rates for the side effect.

choices.label: Read 20 'compliant' cases end-to-end before changing anything
gains: Finds the actual behaviour behind the numbers
choices.likelyOutcome: Often reveals templated first replies or hand-off gaps.

choices.label: Remove the first-response SLA from team-lead scorecards
choices.likelyOutcome: Behaviour shifts; risk of real response delays if nothing replaces it.

relevantConcepts.name: Goodhart's law
relevantConcepts.explanation: A metric that becomes a target can stop measuring what you care about.

relevantConcepts.name: Map vs territory
relevantConcepts.explanation: Dashboards are simplified maps of what customers experience.

relevantConcepts.name: Signal vs noise
relevantConcepts.explanation: Check whether a CSAT change is a real shift before reacting.

debrief: B first is usually the strongest move — you can't fix behaviour you haven't looked at. A and C are both reasonable follow-ups, ideally as paired metrics (speed + quality) rather than swapping one target for another.
reflectionQuestion: Which of your metrics have you not checked against raw cases in the last month?

title: Your best engineer wants to manage
scenario: Illustrative. Arjun is your most technically capable support engineer. He's asked to become a team lead. He's excellent with complex cases but sometimes impatient with colleagues who ask basic questions. A lead role is open now.

choices.label: Promote him now and support him with coaching
costs: You may lose your best technical resolver
choices.likelyOutcome: Can work well if he wants the people work, not just the title.

choices.label: Offer a trial: lead a small pod for a quarter with clear expectations
gains: Tests the fit with lower stakes
choices.likelyOutcome: Both of you learn whether the role suits him.

choices.label: Propose a senior technical path instead
gains: Keeps his expertise where it's strongest
costs: He may see it as a 'no'
Requires a real technical career path to exist
choices.likelyOutcome: Works only if the path has genuine scope and status.

relevantConcepts.name: Stretching high performers
relevantConcepts.explanation: Top performers often get the least management attention.

relevantConcepts.name: Coaching questions
relevantConcepts.explanation: Ask what draws him to the role before deciding for him.

relevantConcepts.name: Concentration risk
relevantConcepts.explanation: Moving your best resolver creates a single-point-of-failure gap.

debrief: Each option is defensible. The best signal is his answer to 'What would make you want to do this role in a year?' If the answer is about people, B or A; if it's about recognition or pay, C may serve him better.
reflectionQuestion: Have you asked your strongest person what they want next, or assumed it?

title: Build or buy an AI knowledge assistant?
scenario: Illustrative. Your support team wants an AI assistant that answers agent questions from internal knowledge articles. A vendor tool can be live in a month. Your internal engineering team says they can build one in a quarter using retrieval over your documents. Your articles are partly outdated.

choices.label: Buy the vendor tool
choices.likelyOutcome: Fast start; quality limited by your content either way.

choices.label: Build internally
costs: Engineering capacity is borrowed from elsewhere
choices.likelyOutcome: Good fit if AI tooling becomes a core capability.

choices.label: Fix the knowledge base first, then decide
gains: Every option improves with better content
choices.likelyOutcome: Raises the ceiling for whichever tool you choose.

relevantConcepts.name: RAG quality depends on documents
relevantConcepts.explanation: Retrieval over outdated articles gives confident outdated answers.

relevantConcepts.name: Build vs buy
relevantConcepts.explanation: Build what differentiates you; buy what doesn't.

relevantConcepts.name: Evaluate before shipping
relevantConcepts.explanation: Agree a test set of real questions before choosing.

debrief: C combined with a small evaluation set of real agent questions lets you compare A and B on evidence. Many teams start with A for speed and revisit B if the capability becomes strategic.
reflectionQuestion: What would you put in a 20-question test set to judge any AI assistant for your team?

title: A deadline you think is unrealistic
scenario: Illustrative. Your director commits to a major customer that a new escalation process will be live across all shifts in two weeks. You believe it needs five weeks to train night shift properly. The commitment has already been made.

choices.label: Disagree privately with data, then commit fully to whatever is decided
costs: You may still have to deliver an unrealistic plan
choices.likelyOutcome: Often leads to a scoped compromise.

choices.label: Propose a phased launch: day shift in two weeks, night shift in five
gains: Meets part of the commitment honestly
costs: Director must reset expectations with the customer
choices.likelyOutcome: Usually accepted if framed around customer risk.

choices.label: Deliver in two weeks with whatever training is possible
costs: Team learns that warnings don't matter
choices.likelyOutcome: On-time launch with a quality dip that lands on customers.

relevantConcepts.name: Disagree and commit
relevantConcepts.explanation: Raise disagreement clearly once, then commit — commitment without real disagreement is just silence.

relevantConcepts.name: Pre-mortem
relevantConcepts.explanation: Imagining failure surfaces the night-shift risk in concrete terms.

relevantConcepts.name: Answer first
relevantConcepts.explanation: Lead with the recommendation, then the evidence.

debrief: A and B work well together: disagree with specifics, propose a phased alternative, then commit to the final call. C avoids conflict now and transfers the cost to customers and your team later.
reflectionQuestion: What's the cost of raising a concern now versus after it has gone wrong?

title: Forty alerts before lunch
scenario: Illustrative. Your team's monitoring channel produces about forty device-offline alerts each morning. Most clear on their own within an hour. Last week a real outage was buried in the noise for three hours. The team wants to mute the channel until noon.

choices.label: Mute until noon as the team suggests
costs: Real incidents in the morning go unseen
choices.likelyOutcome: Quieter mornings; the next real outage is found by a customer.

choices.label: Only alert when offline lasts over an hour or hits many devices at once
costs: Slower detection of genuine single-device issues
choices.likelyOutcome: Much less noise; thresholds need review after a few weeks.

choices.label: Assign a rotating 'alert owner' each morning
choices.likelyOutcome: Better than nobody watching, but fatigue persists.

relevantConcepts.name: Signal vs noise
relevantConcepts.explanation: Separating actionable work from monitoring noise is a design job, not a willpower job.

relevantConcepts.name: Observability
relevantConcepts.explanation: Good signals tell you what's wrong, not just that something changed.

relevantConcepts.name: Swiss cheese model
relevantConcepts.explanation: Muting removes one layer of defence; know what replaces it.

debrief: B combined with C is a common pattern: reduce noise at the source, and keep a named owner for what remains. A treats the symptom and quietly removes a safety layer.
reflectionQuestion: Which alert or report does your team now ignore by habit?
